functional.text: Riders see nearby available drivers on a map with an ETA before requesting.
A rider requests a ride (pickup, drop-off); the system matches a nearby available driver who accepts.
Drivers send their GPS location every ~4 s; riders track the assigned driver's position live.
Trip lifecycle (accepted, arriving, in progress, completed, cancelled); the fare is charged after the trip.

non_functional.text: Absorb ~250k location updates/s at peak; positions used for matching are at most a few seconds old.
Nearby search p99 < 100 ms; a driver is offered the ride within ~5 s of the request.
Consistency of dispatch: a driver is never assigned to two rides at once and a ride never gets two drivers.
Ride requests and trip state are highly available (99.99%) and durable; payments are charged exactly once.

assumptions.text: 1M drivers online at peak worldwide, 20M trips per day; traffic is local to a city.
A driver who ignores an offer for 15 s is released and the next candidate is tried.

out_of_scope.text: Surge pricing model, ETA machine learning, pooled rides, driver onboarding.

api.request: lat, lng, heading, ts (over the driver's WebSocket)

api.notes: Map pins; served from the geo index.
Conditional update: wins only if still matching.
Live updates are pushed over WebSocket.

data.name: driver_locations
data.fields: city:{id} → GEO set of driver_id → (lat, lng) as geohash score; updated_at
data.why: In-memory geo index, overwritten every 4 s; rebuilt from the next updates if lost.

data.name: driver_state
data.why: Leases with TTL decide who may be offered a ride.

data.name: rides
data.fields: ride_id PK, city, rider_id, driver_id, pickup, dropoff, status, fare, created_at, updated_at
data.why: Transactions and conditional updates for the trip state machine; a partial unique index on driver_id for active statuses enforces one ride per driver; sharded by city.

data.name: outbox / trip_events
data.why: Written in the same transaction as the ride, relayed to Kafka for payments and receipts.

deep_dives.title: Hot cities and sharding the geo index

options.name: One global Redis GEO key
options.cons: one key for 1M drivers is one hot shard and one failure domain

options.name: Shard by city / region, split big cities by geohash prefix
options.pros: traffic is local; scales by adding shards
options.cons: requests near a shard border search two shards

deep_dives.choice: Shard the geo index and dispatch by city; split the biggest cities by a geohash prefix and query neighbouring shards near borders
deep_dives.why: Rides almost never cross cities, so a city is a natural partition. A few megacities hold most drivers, so they get several shards keyed by geohash prefix.

deep_dives.title: Driver ignores or declines the offer

options.name: Wait for an explicit decline
options.cons: a driver who loses signal blocks the ride forever

options.name: Lease TTL of 15 s, then the next candidate
options.pros: progress is guaranteed; nothing to clean up
options.cons: a late accept must be rejected by the conditional update

deep_dives.choice: Lease TTL of 15 s, then offer the next ranked candidate; give up and tell the rider after ~3 rounds
deep_dives.why: Mobile networks drop; a TTL bounds how long any single driver can block a ride. A late accept fails the lease check (the lease is gone or names another ride) and gets 409 'offer expired'.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Location ingestion (250k/s) in the biggest cities (shard the geo index by city and geohash prefix); the matching service per city; the push gateway's open WebSocket connections (1M+ drivers, scale horizontally with sticky routing).
wrapup.failures: If a Redis geo shard dies, a replica takes over and positions refill within 4 s. If the PSP is down, payments queue in Kafka and retry with the same idempotency key. If the push gateway drops a connection, the app reconnects and fetches state with GET /rides/{id}.
wrapup.monitoring: Location update lag, geo index size per city, time to match (p50/p99), offer acceptance rate, unmatched requests, lease expiries, payment failures and outbox relay lag.
wrapup.scale: 10× drivers: more city shards and location service instances; the stream partitions by city; the rides database is already sharded by city.
wrapup.future: Pooled rides, H3-based surge pricing, ETA from a road graph, batch matching (assign many riders to many drivers per city every second).

parts.title: Driver location ingestion
parts.problem: Absorb ~250k GPS location updates per second from 1M online drivers (one every 4 s), keep only the latest position for matching, and stream positions to riders who are watching a trip.

options.name: Write each update to the SQL rides database
options.cons: 250k overwrites/s of data that is stale in 4 s; index churn and replication lag on the transactional store

options.name: Write every update to Kafka first; a consumer updates the index
options.cons: adds a hop and seconds of lag to the one thing matching needs fresh

options.name: Location service overwrites an in-memory geo index and appends to a stream on the side
options.pros: memory-speed writes, freshness ~1 s, history and live tracking hang off the stream
options.cons: positions are lost if the index node dies (they come back within 4 s)

parts.choice: Location service overwrites an in-memory geo index (Redis GEO, sharded by city) and appends to a Kafka location stream on the side
parts.why: Only the last position matters and it is replaced every 4 s, so durability is cheap to give up: a lost index rebuilds itself within one update interval. 250k small writes/s across city shards is easy for Redis; the stream feeds live tracking and trip history without slowing ingestion.

nodes.label: Redis GEO: live driver positions by city

edges.label: positions of drivers on active trips

parts.title: Nearby-driver search
parts.problem: Given a rider's position, return the available drivers within a few km in < 100 ms, while those positions change every 4 s.

options.name: SQL range query on lat and lng columns
options.cons: a B-tree indexes one dimension; a box query scans a whole latitude stripe; does not survive 250k updates/s

options.name: Geohash cells in Redis GEO (sorted set by geohash score)
options.pros: GEOADD/GEOSEARCH built in, O(log n + k), cheap overwrites
options.cons: square cells distort near the poles; you search the cell plus neighbours

options.name: In-memory quadtree per region
options.cons: rebalancing under 250k moves/s is costly; custom code

options.name: Hexagonal grid (H3) or S2 cells with an in-memory map cell → drivers
options.pros: uniform neighbours, good for ETA and surge by cell
options.cons: custom index service to build and operate

parts.choice: Geohash-based Redis GEO, one key per city shard: GEOSEARCH a 2 km radius, expand the ring if fewer than ~10 available drivers
parts.why: 1M positions × ~100 B ≈ 100 MB fits in memory many times over, so the question is update cost, not size. Redis GEO gives cheap overwrites and radius search out of the box; H3 is the upgrade when surge pricing and ETA need uniform cells.

nodes.label: Redis GEO: live driver positions by city

parts.title: Matching and dispatch: one driver, one ride
parts.problem: Concurrent ride requests in the same area all see the same nearest driver. Each driver must get one offer at a time and be assigned at most one ride, and an offer that is ignored must free the driver after ~15 s.

options.name: Broadcast the request to several drivers, first accept wins
options.cons: wastes drivers' attention, many losers get 'ride taken'; still needs an atomic accept

options.name: Lock the driver row in SQL for the offer window
options.cons: holds a database lock for 15 s on the hot path; deadlocks across requests

options.name: Per-driver lease with TTL in Redis + conditional write on accept
options.pros: short, self-expiring locks; no lock held in the database
options.cons: lease expiry and accept can race, so the accept must be a conditional write

options.name: Single-threaded dispatcher per city partition
options.cons: a hot partition in big cities; failover pauses dispatch

parts.choice: Lease the chosen driver with SET driver:{id} ride_id NX PX 15000 and send one offer; accept succeeds only if the lease still names this ride (atomic compare-and-set to on_trip) and the conditional UPDATE rides … WHERE status = 'matching' wins, backed by a partial unique index on rides(driver_id) for active statuses
parts.why: The lease stops two matchers offering the same driver, and the TTL frees a driver who ignores the offer with no cleanup job. Two guarantees remain: the conditional update gives a ride one driver, and checking the lease on accept plus the unique index on active rides gives a driver one ride, even when a late accept for an expired offer arrives after the driver was re-leased.

parts.title: Trip state and payments handoff
parts.problem: Drive each trip through a durable state machine (matching → accepted → arriving → in_progress → completed / cancelled) and charge the rider exactly once after completion, even if the payment provider is slow or down.

options.name: Charge the card inside the 'complete trip' request
options.cons: PSP latency and outages block the driver; a retry after a timeout can double-charge

options.name: Distributed transaction across trips and payments
options.cons: the PSP does not take part in 2PC; locks across services

options.name: Commit the state change and an outbox row in one transaction; a payment worker charges with an idempotency key
options.pros: trip flow never waits on the PSP; retries are safe
options.cons: payment completes seconds later; needs reconciliation

parts.choice: Transactional outbox: the trip service commits the transition plus a 'trip_completed' event, a relay publishes it to Kafka and a payment worker charges with Idempotency-Key = ride_id
parts.why: Trip state must never be lost (N4), but the charge can lag by seconds. The outbox removes the dual-write problem, and the idempotency key makes at-least-once delivery safe against double charges.
